svg.desc: Banner for a paper answering Bai and Li's question about the uniform global dispersal model. Left: the total equilibrium population M(d) of the paper's exact three-level habitat (resource 1/20, 25/12 and 329/10 on areas 2405/3504, 5/16 and 1/876), plotted against the dispersal rate d on a logarithmic axis. The curve starts and ends at the mean resource 347/480, rises to a first peak near d = 1.99 (M about 1.00076), dips to the exactly certified minimum M(3) = 1, rises to a second peak near d = 15.1 (M about 1.053) and falls again. Right: the mechanism behind the general theorem. With background resource 1 and rare patches of richness 100, 100000 and 100000000, each patch adds a separate first-order population bump that peaks near half its richness, so N patches give N peaks. The curves are computed from the paper's formulas; maxima are numerical and the effects are tiny, so the result is qualitative.
svg.text: Total population can peak again and again as dispersal changes
The peaks are real but tiny: the first peak above rises only about 0.08% over the dip at d = 3
Total population M(d), exact three-level habitat (Theorem 2)
levels 1/20, 25/12, 329/10; richest on 1/876 of the area
Rare rich patches add separate bumps (Figure 2)
first-order gain from each patch peaks near d ≈ r/2
dispersal rate d (log scale): N patches give N peaks
